In brief

Parody. "And lo, there entered one of the clan of the O'Molloys […] heir of the noble line of Lambert": this single sentence does little more than introduce two men who are now entering Kiernan's pub, J. J. O'Molloy and Ned Lambert. The writing recalls the late medieval or early modern tone struck in another very short parodic interruption, the one that introduced Bloom for the first time.

At more length

In that earlier passage, Bloom was called "the son of Rory," referring to either a late 16th century Irish chieftain or an early 17th century nephew of his who held an English knighthood. That passage clothes our hero in knightly armor and calls him "O'Bloom" to echo the "Ó" names that became popular in Ireland in the later Middle Ages. This new parody introduces one of "the clan of the O'Molloys." No "Ó" needs to be added to his surname, because J. J. was born into one of the many nationalist families that adopted the old custom in the 19th century. As a lawyer, O'Molloy is called "his majesty's counsel learned in the law." High-level attorneys in the UK may be appointed "King's Counsel" or "Queen's Counsel" and carry the official designation "His Majesty's Counsel learned in the law," but there is no suggestion in the novel that O'Molloy has earned this high honor. Joyce apparently calls on the phrase here to paint him as a noble warrior serving a monarch—perhaps thinking of the younger Rory's status as a knight.

The parody begins with an antiquated expression, "And lo," that Joyce used earlier to begin another parody: "And lo, as they quaffed their cup of joy." He then echoes Ireland's pre-English past with "clan" and strikes a vaguely medieval tone in "withal," which came into English usage in the later Middle Ages. This word precedes an ironic undercutting of O'Molloy's "comely" aristocratic appearance: "a comely hero of white face yet withal somewhat ruddy." The sense seems to be that lords and ladies can be spotted by their beautiful untanned skin, but that facts do not perfectly cooperate with the ideal in this case.

The parody ends by observing that O'Molloy is accompanied by "the prince and heir of the noble line of Lambert." For this throwaway detail Joyce did not bother to add much atmospheric coloring.

Incidentally, the first edition of the novel adds an extraneous apostrophe to "O'Molloys," turning what clearly should be a plural into a possessive. This mistake was amended in the Odyssey Press editions of the 1930s, and the American Modern Library editions from 1934 to 1961 likewise do away with it. But in one of its strangely arbitrary and all too frequent returns to early precedents, the Gabler edition restores the absurd apostrophe. It is as if, imitating the practice of many subliterate American homeowners, Gabler imagines the family posting a sign at their front door reading, The Clan of the O'Molloy's. He might reply that the mistake was Joyce's (Cyclops refers also to "the young chief of the O'Bergan's," and that one remains in most editions), but come now—what are editors for if not to save authors from stupid oversights like these?

John Hunt 2026
